questions.question: What is 'Biodiversity' or 'Biological Diversity'?
options: The immense variety of flora and fauna, diverse in form and function, closely integrated in a system through networks of interdependencies
The total number of domestic cattle in a village
The commercial timber exported from national forests
The artificial planting of identical eucalyptus trees
questions.explanation: Biodiversity (biological diversity) denotes the immense variety of flora, fauna, and microorganisms co-existing within terrestrial, marine, and aquatic ecosystems. These organisms, though remarkably diverse in morphological form and ecological function, are integrated into a single life-support network through complex biogeochemical cycles and food webs. Humans form an inseparable part of this web and depend directly on other species for oxygen, water purification, fertile soil formation, pollination, and timber.

questions.question: India is home to approximately what percentage of the total number of species in the world, estimated at 1.6 million?
questions.explanation: India is recognized internationally as one of the world's 12 designated mega-biodiversity nations. Despite occupying only 2.4% of the Earth's total terrestrial land surface, India harbours nearly 8% of the world's total recorded living biological species, numbering an estimated 1.6 million documented species of plants and animals. Over 47,000 plant species (with roughly 15,000 endemic flowering plants) and more than 81,000 faunal species have been catalogued, reflecting extraordinarily diverse forest and wetland ecosystems.

questions.question: In which year was the Asiatic Cheetah officially declared extinct in India?
questions.explanation: The Asiatic Cheetah (Acinonyx jubatus venaticus), renowned as the world's fastest land mammal capable of sprinting up to 112 km/h, was once widespread across the arid grasslands and open scrub forests of central and northern India. However, relentless royal sport hunting, bounty-killing during the British colonial era, and acute habitat fragmentation depleted their prey base, causing their catastrophic collapse. The Government of India officially declared the Asiatic Cheetah extinct within Indian territory in 1952.

questions.question: According to the IUCN classification, what are 'Endangered Species'?
options: Species that are found in every home
Species that reproduce only in winter
Species that have already vanished from the planet
Species whose population has declined and which are in danger of extinction if current negative factors continue to operate
questions.explanation: According to the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) Red List criteria, Endangered Species are defined as taxa whose surviving populations have declined to critically low levels and are in immediate danger of biological extinction if ongoing threatening factors continue unabated. Examples highlighted in the NCERT curriculum include the blackbuck, Indian wild ass, Indian rhinoceros, lion-tailed macaque, and sangai (brow-antlered deer of Manipur), all of which require urgent statutory in-situ habitat protection.

questions.question: Which of the following is an example of an 'Endemic Species' in India?
questions.explanation: According to IUCN classification, Endemic Species are floral or faunal species that are found exclusively in specific, isolated geographical pockets and are naturally absent everywhere else on Earth. Geographical isolation (such as island barriers, mountain chasms, or dense desert boundaries) prevents genetic interbreeding. Classic Indian endemic species catalogued by NCERT include the Andaman teal, Nicobar pigeon, Andaman wild pig, and Mithun (gayal) found strictly in the dense hill forests of Arunachal Pradesh.

questions.question: In which year was the comprehensive Indian Wildlife (Protection) Act implemented to provide legal protection to animal habitats and prohibit hunting?
questions.explanation: The comprehensive Indian Wildlife (Protection) Act was enacted by Parliament in 1972 in response to nationwide alarm over rampant poaching and habitat destruction. The landmark legislation established a statutory all-India framework for wildlife conservation: it completely banned commercial hunting of endangered species, provided legal protection to notified critical habitats by establishing National Parks and Wildlife Sanctuaries, and severely restricted trade in wildlife carcasses, hides, ivory, and derived medicinal products.

questions.question: In which year was 'Project Tiger', one of the well-publicised wildlife campaigns in the world, launched in India?
questions.explanation: Project Tiger was launched by the Government of India in 1973 in collaboration with the World Wildlife Fund (WWF). A national tiger census in 1972 revealed that the wild tiger population had suffered an alarming crash from an estimated 55,000 tigers at the turn of the 20th century to a mere 1,827 individuals due to rampant poaching for tiger bones in traditional Chinese medicine, skin trade, and prey depletion. Project Tiger established dedicated core-buffer tiger reserves across diverse bioclimatic zones.

questions.question: Which of the following is correctly matched regarding Tiger Reserves in India?
options: Corbett National Park - Uttarakhand, Sundarbans - West Bengal, Periyar - Kerala
questions.explanation: Corbett National Park in Uttarakhand (established in 1936 as Hailey National Park, India's oldest), Sundarbans National Park in West Bengal (home to unique mangrove Royal Bengal tigers), Bandhavgarh in Madhya Pradesh, Sariska in Rajasthan, Manas in Assam, and Periyar Tiger Reserve in Kerala are flagship protected reserves established under Project Tiger. These reserves operate on a core-buffer model, strictly prohibiting human interference in core breeding zones to allow viable populations of apex predators to recover.

questions.question: Under the Wildlife Act amendments of 1980 and 1986, which smaller creatures were added to the list of protected species for the first time?
options: Several hundred butterflies, moths, beetles, and one dragonfly
questions.explanation: Under landmark legislative amendments made to the Indian Wildlife (Protection) Act in 1980 and 1986, the statutory conservation umbrella was officially broadened beyond charismatic large mammals and birds to recognize smaller, ecologically indispensable invertebrates. Several hundred species of butterflies, moths, beetles, and one dragonfly were placed on protected schedules. In 1991, plants were added to the Act for the first time, beginning with six rare medicinal plant species placed under statutory trade bans.

questions.question: Forests that are regarded as the most valuable for conservation of forest and wildlife resources and constitute more than half of total forest land are called:
questions.explanation: Under Indian forest administration, Reserved Forests are designated as the most valuable and protected category of public forest lands for the long-term conservation of timber, soil, and wildlife resources. Constituting more than half (over 50%) of the nation's total recorded forest area, Reserved Forests enjoy the highest degree of statutory protection under the Indian Forest Act: all commercial logging, cattle grazing, and individual human access are strictly prohibited unless expressly permitted by the state forest department.

questions.question: Almost one-third of the total forest area in India is declared as Protected Forests, which means they are:
options: Completely open for timber logging by private companies
Protected from any further depletion, while allowing limited customary rights to local people
questions.explanation: Protected Forests constitute almost one-third (approximately 29%) of the total recorded forest area in India. These forest tracts are formally declared and managed by state forest departments with the statutory mandate of preventing any further destruction, encroachment, or ecological degradation. Unlike Reserved Forests, local rural and tribal communities are generally granted regulated usufructuary rights in Protected Forests, allowing them to collect dry firewood, graze cattle, and harvest minor forest produce.

questions.question: Which Indian state has the largest area under permanent forests, constituting 75 percent of its total forest area?
questions.explanation: Madhya Pradesh possesses the largest area under permanent forests in the entire country, accounting for an impressive 75% of its total state forest expanse classified into permanent reserved and protected forest reserves. Other states with substantial proportions of reserved forests include Jammu & Kashmir, Andhra Pradesh, Uttarakhand, Kerala, Tamil Nadu, West Bengal, and Maharashtra, whereas states like Bihar, Haryana, Punjab, Himachal Pradesh, Odisha, and Rajasthan possess high percentages of protected forests.

questions.question: In which regions of India do Unclassed Forests (managed largely by local communities and private individuals) constitute a very high percentage of forest cover?
options: All North-eastern states and parts of Gujarat
questions.explanation: Unclassed Forests represent unclassified woodlands, scrublands, and vast tracts of virgin forest and wasteland that belong to both government departments and private individuals or local tribal communities. Unclassed forests are predominant throughout all North-eastern states (such as Meghalaya, Nagaland, Mizoram, and Assam) and interior parts of Gujarat, where dense natural forests are managed and conserved almost entirely by autonomous tribal village councils through customary clan traditions.

questions.question: The famous 'Chipko Movement' in the Himalayas successfully resisted deforestation by:
options: Villagers hugging trees to prevent commercial loggers from cutting them down
Filing cases in the international court
questions.explanation: The historic Chipko Movement originated in the Garhwal Himalayas of Uttarakhand (notably Reni village in Chamoli district) during the early 1970s. Village women, inspired by Gandhian environmentalist Sunderlal Bahuguna and Chandi Prasad Bhatt, physically clung to and hugged forest trees to block commercial timber contractors from axing them. The movement not only successfully stopped commercial clear-felling across Himalayan watersheds, but also pioneered community-led ecological afforestation with indigenous broadleaf species.

questions.question: The 'Beej Bachao Andolan' (Save the Seeds Movement) and 'Navdanya' in Tehri (Uttarakhand) proved that:
options: Diverse traditional crop production without synthetic chemical fertilizers is economically viable and ecologically sustainable
Hybrid seeds alone can feed the country
All agriculture should be replaced by animal husbandry
Chemical pesticides increase natural soil biodiversity
questions.explanation: The 'Beej Bachao Andolan' (Save the Seeds Movement) and 'Navdanya', spearheaded by traditional agrarian communities in the Tehri Garhwal region of Uttarakhand, demonstrated that reviving diverse indigenous traditional crop seed varieties without synthetic agrochemicals or chemical fertilizers is both economically viable and ecologically sustainable. By reviving traditional multi-cropping systems like 'Barahnaja' (intercropping twelve resilient grain and legume crops), farmers ensured nutritional security and soil vitality.

questions.question: In the Alwar district of Rajasthan, the inhabitants of five villages declared 1,200 hectares of forest as 'Bhairodev Dakav Sonchuri' to:
options: Sell commercial timber to mining companies
Construct a highway across the Aravalli hills
Enforce their own community rules banning hunting and protecting wildlife from external encroachment
questions.explanation: In the Alwar district of Rajasthan, rural inhabitants of five villages took community conservation into their own hands by declaring 1,200 hectares of virgin community forest land as the 'Bhairodev Dakav Sonchuri' (sanctuary). The villagers formulated and strictly enforced their own democratic community regulations: they completely banned commercial hunting and wildlife poaching, and actively prohibited external commercial logging and mining encroachments, protecting wildlife without government bureaucratic intervention.

questions.question: What are 'Sacred Groves' preserved by traditional tribal communities across India?
options: Commercial rubber plantations owned by the state
Artificial botanical gardens in metropolitan cities
Virgin patches of natural forest left untouched and protected due to ancestral religious reverence
Timber logging coupes earmarked for export
questions.explanation: Sacred Groves (known locally as 'Orans' in Rajasthan, 'Devarakadu' in Karnataka, 'Sarnas' in Jharkhand, and 'Kavu' in Kerala) are pristine patches of natural primeval forest left completely untouched and rigorously guarded by indigenous tribal communities due to deep ancestral religious veneration. Indigenous cultures believe that ancestral nature spirits inhabit these sacred woodlands. Consequently, cutting trees, gathering firewood, hunting wild animals, or harming any living organism within the grove is strictly forbidden.

questions.question: The Mundas and Santhals of the Chotanagpur region worship which sacred trees during religious festivities?
questions.explanation: Traditional tribal communities across India harbor profound spiritual reverences for specific indigenous trees. The Mundas and Santhals of the mineral-rich Chotanagpur plateau (Jharkhand, Odisha, West Bengal) revere and worship the Mahua (Madhuca latifolia, prized for fragrant edible flowers and oil seeds) and Kadamba (Anthocephalus cadamba) trees during religious festivals, while tribal communities in Odisha and Bihar venerate the Tamarind (Tamarindus indica) and Mango (Mangifera indica) during wedding rituals.

questions.question: Which Indian state passed the first formal government resolution for Joint Forest Management (JFM) in 1988?
questions.explanation: The state of Odisha achieved a historic conservation breakthrough by passing the very first formal government resolution for Joint Forest Management (JFM) in 1988. The JFM program institutionalized a democratic partnership between the state forest department and local rural communities, establishing village-level Forest Protection Committees (VPCs) to regenerate, manage, and protect degraded public forest tracts from illegal grazing, logging, and forest fires in return for shared economic and usufructuary benefits.

questions.question: Under the Joint Forest Management (JFM) programme, what benefits do participating village communities receive in return for protecting degraded forests?
options: Rights to non-timber forest produce and a share in the timber harvested upon successful management
Permanent ownership of all forest land
Exemption from all central income taxes
questions.explanation: Under the Joint Forest Management (JFM) institutional framework, local village communities who actively form forest protection committees and guard regenerating degraded public forest lands are legally entitled to substantial usufructuary benefits. Participating households receive intermediate rights to collect non-timber forest produce (NTFP)—such as dry firewood, sal leaves, mahua flowers, medicinal roots, and gums—as well as a designated proportional share in the commercial revenues of mature timber harvests.
